questions.question: Which invariant best describes a cloud-native workload instance?
options: The instance must retain all durable state on its local disk.
The instance is disposable, while its contract, durable state, and operating evidence survive replacement.
The instance is safe only when it runs as a microservice.
The instance must be portable to every cloud provider.
questions.explanation: Disposable compute can be reconciled and replaced. Durable data, configuration, identity, and evidence need explicit owners outside one container.

questions.question: A service peaks at 25,000 requests per second. One pod sustains 1,200 requests per second at the target latency, and the team requires 30% headroom. What is the starting replica estimate?
questions.explanation: ceil(25,000 x 1.30 / 1,200) equals ceil(27.08), so the starting estimate is 28 pods before placement and dependency constraints are checked.

questions.question: Why can four mandatory services at 99.9% availability produce a path near 99.6%?
options: Kubernetes reserves 0.1% for control-plane work.
Availability is added across every hop.
The path succeeds only when every required dependency succeeds, so independent availability probabilities multiply.
A service mesh always consumes 0.3% availability.
questions.explanation: For an all-required path, independent component availability multiplies: 0.999 to the fourth power is about 0.996.

questions.question: What makes a canary release reduce blast radius?
options: The new version uses a different image tag.
A small representative cohort is held until explicit service and business gates pass.
The deployment controller creates every pod at once.
The canary has no access to production dependencies.
questions.explanation: Small exposure helps only when the cohort represents real risk and promotion waits for sufficient evidence with a working rollback action.

questions.question: Which probe should control whether a pod receives new traffic?
options: Startup probe
Readiness probe
Liveness probe
Image scan
questions.explanation: Readiness represents traffic eligibility. Startup delays other probes during initialization, while liveness asks whether restart may repair the process.

questions.question: Why can adding caller replicas make a slow dependency incident worse?
options: Replicas disable service discovery.
More callers can create more concurrent requests and retries against the already saturated dependency.
Every replica requires a separate database schema.
The scheduler stops enforcing timeouts.
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling increases potential concurrency. Without deadlines, admission control, and retry budgets, it amplifies pressure downstream.

questions.question: A write times out and the client did not receive a response. What is the safe retry contract?
options: Assume the write failed and create a new operation ID.
Retry at every network layer until one succeeds.
Reconcile the original idempotency key because the outcome is unknown, then retry only within policy.
Move the write to a liveness probe.
questions.explanation: A timeout does not prove that the effect failed. Reconciliation by the original key avoids duplicating an operation that already committed.

questions.question: Which observation most directly supports an automated rollout decision?
options: A dashboard exists for cluster CPU.
The new version has a recent build timestamp.
Representative canary service and business SLIs remain within explicit promotion and rollback thresholds.
All pods have unique names.
questions.explanation: Rollout automation needs version-attributed, representative behavior tied to a decision threshold and action, not merely infrastructure visibility.
